column2: On the afternoon of the third day, the Seventh Lady accompanied Luo Sijie to consult Wu Tiekou. He lived on Second Road, whose English name had been Rope Walk Road, translated into Chinese as Towpath Road. In the early days, boats could still use Yangjing Creek, but the shallow water made towing necessary. When the towpath was turned into a road, it retained that name. The local people could not manage the English street names, so they called Garden Lane, the first road opened, First Road. The next to the south became Second Road, followed by Third, Fourth and Fifth Roads, all running east and west, down to Yangjing Creek. Two years earlier, First Road had been renamed Nanjing Road and Second Road Hangzhou Road. Someone pointed out to the foreigners that there were two waterways between Nanjing and Hangzhou, the Yangtze and the Grand Canal. Since Nanjing was on the lower Yangtze, the name of a major port farther upstream would make a more fitting companion to Nanjing Road. Second Road was therefore renamed Jiujiang Road, and Third Road, formerly Customs Road, naturally became Hankou Road. Shanghai people were accustomed to the old names, however, and continued to say First Road and Second Road.

Second Road had been opened early, and its shops and businesses had long flourished. Wu Tiekou's place for receiving clients was in Fuhou Lane: the first house on the right. Two stone-gated houses had been joined together, making a large reception hall. Its walls were covered with inscribed plaques presented by high officials, wealthy merchants and distinguished men. Hu Xueyan had given one himself, bearing the words “Supreme Mastery of Ziping Astrology.” It hung on the north partition, beside a door leading to Wu's consulting room. Wu had a square face, large ears and a moustache that spread down on either side. He was only a little over thirty, but his large dark-crystal spectacles made him look older. He wore a lined robe of date-red satin beneath a black jacket patterned with round floral medallions. An enormous stone called pinxia was set in the band of his blue-satin cap. His fingernails were very long. On his left thumb he wore an archer's ring of Han jade, on his right ring finger a platinum ring set with a square diamond; a bright gold watch chain crossed his chest. He was dressed like a fashionable rake. “Mrs Gu!” He rose to greet them, four purses of different sizes dangling beneath his jacket. Removing his spectacles, he smiled. “How well you look.” “With a bijie period like this, how could I not?” She indicated Luo. “This is a dear friend of mine, surnamed Luo. You may call her Sister Luo.” “Certainly. Sister Luo. Please sit down, both of you.” There were two stools beside the rosewood desk, one opposite Wu and one to his left. The Seventh Lady took the former, indicating that Luo should sit beside him for ease of conversation. Wu put on his spectacles, settled into his rosewood armchair, rolled back his sleeves and took up his brush. Having asked Luo's birth year, month, day and hour, he wrote her Four Pillars on a writing tablet: ji-si, xin-wei, jia-zi, jia-zi. He added marks and annotations, laid down the brush and studied them intently.

He studied them for a full quarter of an hour. From the side, Luo could see his eyes blinking rapidly behind the dark lenses, and she began to feel uneasy. “Mr Wu,” she said at last, unable to contain herself, “is my destiny bad?” He removed his spectacles and looked at her. “What a pity!” Then he turned to the Seventh Lady and repeated with emphasis, “A very great pity!” “What is it? Please tell us frankly. A sensible person asks about misfortune, not good fortune. Sister Luo is broad-minded. There is no need to spare her feelings.” Wu nodded heavily, set his spectacles aside and pointed with his brush. “Sister Luo, yours is a Wood destiny. Beneath your day stem lies a Direct Seal, and the hour is also jia-zi: Wood has a fellow to support it and a Seal to shelter it. Judging by the day and hour pillars alone, this is a superior configuration, one that turns misfortune into blessing and danger into good luck.” Luo did not understand “superior configuration,” but she could tell that her destiny was good. “Please go on.” “Wood born in summer, in a si-Fire year as well: this tree would normally find it hard to survive. Fortunately, zi-Water nourishes it. Not only can it live; it is a great tree. Metal, Wood, Water, Fire and Earth are all present, and so are Wealth, Officer, Seal and the Food God. Moreover, these are a Direct Officer and a Direct Seal. If this were a man's horoscope, he would be like Lord Pan Wenrong of Suzhou: first in the imperial examination, a chief minister, living to eighty with children and grandchildren all around him, enjoying endless honour and riches. A pity it is a woman's destiny!”

Before Luo could speak, the Seventh Lady protested loudly. “What is wrong with a woman's destiny? Are examination champions and chief ministers not born of women?” “Do not be angry, Mrs Gu,” Wu replied calmly. “When I say it is a pity, I do not mean that Sister Luo's destiny is bad. Heaven would not forgive me if I called a horoscope like this bad.” Her anger gave way to pleasure. “Then what is there to regret? Please, Mr Wu, tell us honestly.” “I had intended to judge the horoscope on its merits and speak plainly. Now I hardly dare.” “Why not?” “With your temper, Mrs Gu, if I said something unwelcome, you might slap me. I could not afford such a loss of dignity.” “I beg your pardon!” She laughed apologetically. “Rest assured. Explain yourself clearly, and of course I shan't lose my temper.” Wu called for his water pipe, then told his young attendant to bring a fruit platter for the ladies. Repeatedly protesting against all this trouble, the Seventh Lady nevertheless summoned her maid to bring her silver water pipe. She lit a paper spill and began smoking with leisurely, bubbling draws. She and Wu were playing their duet with a perfect understanding, and Luo was already taken in. Desperate to learn what was so regrettable, she grew impatient at this interruption, even resenting the Seventh Lady's failure to consider her anxiety. Unable to say so openly, she pretended to cough, as though the pipe smoke were choking her, to hint that her friend might stop.

“Open the window,” Wu ordered. He put down his pipe and took up his brush again, first looking at the Seventh Lady to secure her attention. “A woman's horoscope must be read differently from a man's. In a woman's destiny, the element that controls her represents the Husband Star. Thus what we call the Direct Officer and Indirect Officer in a man's horoscope both stand for husbands in a woman's. That is a fundamental rule. You must understand it to see why Sister Luo's horoscope is regrettable.” The Seventh Lady knew something of astrology and followed him. Luo understood less, but, eager for what came next, nodded faintly too. “Metal controls Wood. This xin-Metal in the month pillar is the Husband Star for jia-Wood. The trouble is that there is another jia in the hour pillar. We have a name for that: Two Women Contending for One Husband.” The women exchanged a simultaneous glance. Luo's look conveyed a request, and the Seventh Lady spoke for her. “You mean another woman will compete with Sister Luo?” “Exactly.” “Can she win?” “If she could, there would be nothing to regret. When two women contend for one husband, the stronger wins. On the surface, each is jia-zi, with zi-Water generating jia-Wood. It is like children fighting: a parent comes out to help the child on one side, and another parent speaks up on the other. They seem evenly matched.” “Yes, yes, I understand!” Luo said repeatedly. “By the usual rule, Sister Luo, the jia-zi in the hour pillar ought not to beat you. Your Husband Star is right beside you: the pavilion nearest the water catches the moon first. You should have the advantage. Unfortunately, there is the configuration called geng-zi wang-wei. Chen, xu, chou and wei are the Earth of the four seasons, and Earth generates Metal. On the other side, Wealth benefits the Officer. That is excellent for the Husband Star but disastrous for you, because Wealth Damages the Seal. Imagine children fighting when one has parents and the other has lost theirs and is an orphan. Could the orphan defeat the other child?”

The Seventh Lady, who could follow the explanation, thought it marvellous. “Let me look, Mr Wu.” He turned the tablet round, angling it slightly towards Luo so that both could see. After studying it, the Seventh Lady pointed things out to her friend. “Look. This wei beneath geng is Earth. It is right beside your zi, which is Water, and Water controls Earth. Water is Wealth and Earth is the Seal, hence Wealth Damages the Seal. There is nothing to be done. You are destined to lose to the other woman.” “And what happens if I lose?” That, of course, was for Wu to answer. “Become a concubine.” The words were uncompromising. Repelled by his cold, unfeeling tone, Luo raised her voice. “And if I refuse to become a concubine?” “You will bring death to your husband.” “I have already lost one.” “You must still become a concubine.” “I insist on being a principal wife!” “Then you will still bring death. Every man you marry will die.” Luo's face went white with anger. “I don't believe…” Wu's iron certainty met an equally unyielding resistance. Seeing a quarrel about to break out, the Seventh Lady quickly tugged Luo's clothes. “Better defy your father than defy your fate. Hear Mr Wu out. If he makes no sense, there will be time enough to contradict him.” “If I make no sense, Mrs Gu, Sister Luo may slap me and I shall not lift a hand.” Wu pointed to the tablet. “Her husband's death can also be seen here. The Seal represents shelter. At home a woman depends on her father; once married, on her husband. The Seal is her support. If her husband dies, has that support not collapsed?” He raised his eyes to observe her reaction.

Luo's expression had softened somewhat. The Seventh Lady asked, “But why must she still become a concubine?” “Because after wei-Earth has overcome the first zi-Water, it goes on to overcome the second. There is no escaping it. If she truly refuses to become a concubine, there is nothing to be done. Everyone has their own aspirations; we cannot force them. But then there is no need to examine the Wealth, Officer and Food God in the earlier part of the horoscope.” “Why not?” “What use are they if the person is no longer alive?” Luo was badly startled. “Mr Wu, do you mean I shall die if I refuse to become a concubine?” “Certainly. Wei-Earth overcomes one zi-Water after another. Suppose jia-Wood refuses to retreat and confronts it. Very well: Wood controls Earth, and jia-Wood has assistance, so its strength is considerable. But look at wei-Earth. The ji-Earth in the year pillar supports it. That is not even the most important thing: the greatest power is si-Fire, for Fire generates Earth, supplying it without end. Which side is stronger? In the interaction of the Five Elements, what fails to overcome its opponent is overcome in turn. This wei-Earth is hard as rock, on which nothing can grow. If jia-Wood challenges it, it is like trying to split a mountain with a piece of timber. The timber breaks; the mountain remains.” Luo looked like a defeated fighting cock. Her fierce insistence on being a principal wife had vanished completely, although inwardly she still resented becoming a concubine.

The Seventh Lady now turned to the favourable side. “Then she will be all right if she becomes a concubine?” “It is not merely a matter of being all right. Only by becoming a concubine—that is, by accepting xin-Metal as her Husband Star—can we begin to discuss the benefits of those four characters at the beginning.” “You mean the four characters of the year and month pillars?” “Yes. Earth generating Metal is like a mother and child. Once Wood has married Metal, they belong to the same family. There is no reason for further conflict…” “Mr Wu,” the Seventh Lady interrupted, “I was asking about the benefits of those four characters.” “They are endless. The finest feature of this horoscope is the Food God represented by si-Fire. In a horoscope, male or female, the Food God always means intelligence and good looks. It is what the self produces. Here the Food God generates Wealth in the two Earth signs, ji and wei; Wealth generates the xin-Officer. That is the fortune of a woman who advances her husband. In other words, the brilliance of the Husband Star depends entirely on this Food God that she produces.” “Most enlightening!” The Seventh Lady turned to Luo. “Sister Luo, is there anything else you would like to ask Mr Wu?”

Luo hesitated, then gave her a look. Understanding that she wanted a private word, the Seventh Lady rose and went aside with her. Luo whispered, “Seventh Sister, ask him what sort of destiny would suit mine.” “I understand.” Returning to her seat, the Seventh Lady asked, “If she marries, Mr Wu, what sort of destiny should the man have?” “Metal, naturally.” “What about Earth?” She gave him the faintest signal with her eyes. Wu was extremely quick-witted. “Earth generates Metal. Better still,” he replied at once. “Oh.” She sounded as though she attached no particular importance to it, then turned to Luo. “Anything else?” “Nothing comes to mind just now.” That answer showed that Luo already believed Wu's pronouncements to be infallible, and that she had much more on her mind to ask him. The Seventh Lady felt that her plan now had at least a seventy or eighty per cent chance of success. It was time to stop. She beckoned her maid to bring her purse, preparing to take out a banknote to pay his fee.

“Thank you very much for today, Mr Wu. But I must trouble you to write out a detailed reading of her whole life.” “Well…” Wu looked reluctant. “I am afraid I may not have time just now.” “Miss a couple of dinners with courtesans, and you will have time.” He laughed. “That too is ordained by my destiny. With peach blossoms all along my path, if I don't dine with courtesans, I shall have to dine with the King of Hell. It would be a poor bargain.” He was half joking. The Seventh Lady pursed her lips in disdain. “I know you are busy. A delay doesn't matter, but the reading must be very thorough.” “As long as there is no time limit, careful work is certain to produce a fine result.” “Good.” Sorting through her banknotes, she asked, “How much should we pay you?” “You know my rules, Mrs Gu. I depend entirely on the good fortune of my distinguished clients. If a destiny is bad, I won't read it however much I am offered. If it is good, I am too embarrassed to ask much. Give whatever you please. You would never let me give my work away.” “Giving away a destiny would be giving away a life!” She laid a fifty-tael note on the desk. “I hope you won't think it too little.” “It is a little on the low side. But I certainly shan't object.” “I know that for a horoscope like Sister Luo's, this is not enough. We are bound to consult you again. We shall make it up to you later.”

As they took their leave, the Seventh Lady invited Luo to have a Western meal and watch Japanese conjuring tricks. Luo pleaded a headache and insisted on going home. Her friend understood: Wu's categorical pronouncements had stirred up endless thoughts, and Luo wanted to consider them privately. She did not press the invitation. They rode together in the Gu carriage, and on reaching her own house she told the coachman to take Luo home. After ten that evening, Gu Yingchun and Hu Xueyan returned together from an engagement at a courtesan's house in Baoshan Street. Knowing that the Seventh Lady had taken Luo to have her fortune told that day, Hu had come expressly for the news. “This Wu Tiekou really has some ability. He made even me believe him.” It was the Seventh Lady herself who had instructed him to say that Luo must become a concubine. If she could accept her own invention as truth when she heard it from someone else, his argument must have been extraordinary. Gu was now as eager as Hu to hear it. “It makes me laugh to think of it. Wu was most blunt. Every other word was either ‘bring death to your husband’ or ‘become a concubine.’ Sister Luo was truly angry. But do you know what happened in the end?” “Don't ask us,” Gu said. “Just tell the story.” “In the end she privately asked me to find out what destiny would make a good match for her. Wu said Metal, naturally. I asked, ‘What about Earth?’ That is where I really admire him. It was nothing remarkable that he understood my meaning; what was clever was his instant answer: ‘Earth generates Metal. Better still.’” “Little Uncle,” Gu said with a smile, “it looks as though happy events will come in pairs.” “It all depends on Seventh Sister's help,” Hu replied, beaming. “Did you hear?” Gu said to his wife. “Everything is in your hands.”

“Leave it to me! But we must not rush. Sister Luo is shrewder than anyone. If she detects a clue and decides we are deceiving her, she will refuse to listen to another word. I must wait for her to speak to me about it. If I raise it myself, I may give the game away.” “Quite right.” Hu nodded earnestly. “I am in no hurry.” “In that case, Little Uncle, you might as well return to Hangzhou first. Leave her alone for a while, and things may move faster.” Hu thought briefly. “I shall go back and return after the festival.” “Good. You can make some preparations there. Tell your mother first.” “She knows Sister Luo too. She is sure to agree.” “And Aunt?” “She has said herself that she needs someone to help her.” “You must make quite sure of her agreement,” the Seventh Lady urged solemnly. “If Aunt disapproves, I shan't arrange this. I have known her for years. It would not be worth creating ill feeling between us.” The Seventh Lady got on extremely well with everyone in Hu's household and was deeply respected because she knew exactly how to conduct herself in such delicate matters. Hu did not resent her frankness. He promised to tell his wife the truth and never leave the Seventh Lady in an awkward position later. “Then I shall wait for your letter.” “Good. I expect to leave in three or four days. Do you think I ought to see her again first?” “Of course. You can visit her every day if you like. Only be sure not to mention the fortune-telling.” Gu, who had said little, reminded his wife, “A full bowl of rice is easily eaten; a sweeping promise is hard to fulfil. Don't imagine you are absolutely certain. If Sister Luo really has plans for her future, she must be anxious to discuss them with you. But she may be embarrassed to come seeking your advice. You ought to visit her. That is how to show consideration for a friend.”

The Seventh Lady willingly accepted her husband's suggestion and drove over the following morning. It was already after ten when she arrived. Quite a few embroidery workers were still sitting in the reception room, but Old Ma alone was attending to them. “Where is your mistress?” “She says she is unwell and hasn't come downstairs.” Old Ma smiled helplessly. “I am all at sea on my own.” “I shall help.” The Seventh Lady sat in Luo's usual place. Having visited several times and taken a hand before, she was not entirely unfamiliar with issuing materials and payments and inspecting finished work. Whenever a difficulty arose, she sent the maid upstairs to ask before deciding. Everything was settled within half an hour. “I shall go up and see her. What is wrong with her?” she asked the maid. “She is not ill,” the girl whispered. “She cried all last night, until her eyes were swollen.” Startled, the Seventh Lady asked quickly, “Why?” “I don't know. I didn't dare ask.” She said no more, lifted her skirt and went upstairs. Luo's bedroom was completely dark. Guessing that the light hurt her red, swollen eyes, she stopped in the doorway. A voice came from behind the bed curtains.

“Is that Seventh Sister?” “Yes.” “Don't move. Let me get up and help you.” “No, no. I can see a little now.” Holding the doorframe, the Seventh Lady advanced slowly. “Be careful!” Luo was already up. She drew back a corner of the window curtain to let in some light, then turned her own face away. “Thank goodness you came. Old Ma really couldn't manage by himself.” “The light hurts your eyes. Go back behind your bed curtains.” That was what Luo had intended. Besides finding the light painful, she did not want her friend to see how swollen her eyes were. She agreed and returned to bed, telling the maid, who had followed them up, to bring tea and prepare lunch. “Don't trouble yourself. I feel as much at home here as in my own house. If I want anything, I shall tell them.” Sitting on a bench beside the bed, the Seventh Lady asked quietly, “What is the matter?” “I feel miserable.” “What is it that you cannot put aside?” Luo said nothing, and there was no need to ask further. Reaching through the curtains to touch her face, the Seventh Lady found her eyes swollen to the size of apricots, with traces of tears still on her cheeks. “You must stop crying,” she scolded. “A woman's eyes are everything to her. You must look after yourself. What if you cry yourself blind?” “How could I cry myself blind?” Changing the subject, Luo asked, “Where have you come from?” “Home.” The Seventh Lady called to the maid. “Bring a basin of hot water and a fresh towel—new flannel would be best.” She wanted to apply a hot compress to reduce the swelling. While doing so, she told Luo that Hu would soon return to Hangzhou for the festival. They would give him a farewell dinner in the next two or three days, and she wanted Luo to come.

“On what day?” “We must wait until the swelling has gone down and you can go out.” “That will only take a day or two.” “Then let us make it three days from today. Come early. We can eat early, and afterwards I shall take you to the theatre.” “All right.” Just then the clock began to strike. Luo silently counted twelve. “My clock is slow. It is already past noon.” She called to the maid, “Go and hurry the restaurant. The food should have arrived.” “It has.” “Then why didn't you say so? Will it be any good once it is cold?” She began scolding the maid. The Seventh Lady intervened, saying that anger would make deficient fire rise and harm her eyes. Only then did Luo stop. “Bring lunch upstairs,” the Seventh Lady instructed. “I shall eat with your mistress.” When the meal was brought up, Luo got out of bed, but still sat with her back to the light, never allowing her friend to see her eyes. “What has upset you so much? I thought you were a very straightforward person. I never imagined you could brood like this.” “It is not brooding. I resent my miserable fate.” “With a horoscope like yours, you call your fate miserable?” “How can I not? Think, Seventh Sister: either I remain a widow or I become a concubine. The more I think about it, the less I can accept it. I am determined to defy my fate.” “You still seem angry. Let it go. I shall take you to the theatre the day after tomorrow to cheer you up.”

“I don't particularly want to see a play. But I shall certainly come early.” “As long as you do. We can decide about the theatre then. With Little Uncle going to Hangzhou, would you like him to take a letter or anything else?” “Would it be convenient?” “Of course. He has servants and a boat. It belongs to his bureau and is towed by a small steamer, so it is fast and steady.” Luo nodded. Instead of saying whether she had anything to send, she asked about Hu's bureau. The Seventh Lady explained the Shanghai Transport Bureau that served the western campaign. “You know Lord Zuo, who recovered your Hangzhou?” “Yes.” “He is now Governor-General of Shaanxi and Gansu, with tens of thousands of troops fighting there. Conditions are very harsh. They depend entirely on the rear commissariats for supplies. Little Uncle manages one of the most important, the Shanghai Transport Bureau.” “What does it send?” “Everything. The most important things are guns and cannon. Lord Zuo's victories depend entirely on the Western weapons Little Uncle buys for him in Shanghai.” “What else?” “A great deal.” The Seventh Lady counted on her fingers. “Uniforms, food, medicines…” “Medicines have to be sent too?” Luo interrupted. “Of course. Especially in summer. Huoxiang Zhengqi Pills and Biwen Dan are sent by the hundreds and thousands of cases.”

“No wonder!” Luo suddenly understood. “What?” “He told me the other day that he wanted to open a medicine shop. So the rich water is not to flow into someone else's fields.” “There are plenty of other businesses where he could keep the profits in his own hands. But he doesn't dare give them free rein.” “Why?” “He needs people to help him. How can he manage without them?” “Isn't Brother-in-Law Gu a first-rate assistant?” “In outside affairs. He needs a good assistant at home too.” The Seventh Lady gave an example. “Take the coming Dragon Boat Festival. Think of the trouble involved in sending the gifts alone. From princes and great officials in Beijing down to poor relations, the list is enough to frighten you. Leave one person out, and you offend them. Give too little, and you offend them too.” “Give too much, and you can also cause offence,” Luo said. “And perhaps offend more than one person.” “Exactly.” The Seventh Lady said no more.

On the day of Hu's farewell dinner, Luo arrived just after the Seventh Lady had finished lunch. “Have you any time to spare?” she asked at once. “What is it?” “If you have, I should like you to come with me to buy things to send to Hangzhou. And I want someone to write a letter home for me.” Old Ma was readily available, the Seventh Lady thought. Why did Luo want someone else to write her letter? Plainly there was a reason. She said nothing about shopping and asked only about the letter. “What sort of person are you looking for?” “Preferably…” Luo hesitated. “Someone like you.” “I have hardly more learning than you. If you cannot write a letter, neither can I.” She thought for a moment. “There is no need for you to go shopping yourself. Tell me what you want, and I shall send someone. Yingchun will be home soon. I shall press him into service to write the letter.” “That will do.” The Seventh Lady summoned her steward, A’fu, and Luo gave him her instructions. Foodstuffs and household articles, all the foreign and southern merchandise sold in Shanghai, were rare and precious in the interior. The list grew so long that A’fu had to fetch paper and brush. “Thank you, steward.” Luo took out a fifty-tael banknote, but as she was about to hand it over, the Seventh Lady stopped her. “There is no need. I have a shop account book,” Luo said. A’fu would not take the money without his mistress's permission. The Seventh Lady guessed that the account book for collecting goods must have been a gift from Hu. Since Luo did not wish to use it, or accept presents from anyone else, there was no reason to insist. “Very well. As you wish.” Only then did A’fu accept the note and go to make the purchases.

Gu happened to return just then. After a brief rest, his wife conscripted him to write Luo's letter. “This is not an easy assignment,” he said with a smile. “Shall I work like a character-diviner who writes letters for people, putting down each sentence as you dictate it? Or will you give me the general sense, and I shall write it out for you to read and correct?” “Which is easier?” “Taking it down sentence by sentence, naturally.” “Then let us do it the easy way.” “Good. Come with me.” In the study, Gu spread out a sheet of paper and moistened his brush. He first wrote, “Respectfully submitted at the feet of my honoured mother,” then looked up at Luo across the desk. “Brother-in-Law Gu, please tell my mother that I am well in Shanghai and she need not worry. Is her liver-qi trouble any better? She must not stop taking her medicine. I am sending her fifty taels. She must not economize on medicine.” Gu wrote it down. “Yes. What else?” “I am also sending a basket of foreign and southern goods with someone. Will she decide what to distribute among our relatives? She must be sure not to let A’qiao eat too many sweets…” “Who is A’qiao?” “My daughter.”

“Should I mention who is bringing the things?” “No.” “Very well. Anything else?” “Yes.” Luo thought for a moment. “I shall go back to Hangzhou to see her at the Mid-Autumn Festival.” “Anything else?” “She must reply as soon as she receives this letter. And she must ask Mr Wu to write the reply.” “Hu, written with ‘ancient’ and ‘moon,’ or Wu, with ‘mouth’ and ‘heaven’?” “Neither. Wu as in ‘crow.’” “I see. Anything else?” “No.” Gu finished and read the letter aloud. Luo was satisfied. When he came to address the envelope, he asked how she wanted it written. “What is the proper form, Brother-in-Law Gu?” “The usual form is, ‘Respectfully troubling So-and-so to deliver this to So-and-so at a convenient opportunity,’ with ‘Entrusted by So-and-so’ below.” “Could we simply write, ‘Respectfully requesting delivery at a convenient opportunity’?” Of course they could. Gu had asked again because she had already said there was no need to identify the bearer, and he wanted confirmation. He could now be certain that she was deliberately avoiding Hu's name. Her reason for doing so was intriguing.

Only when she was about to leave did Luo speak to Hu. “Mr Hu, I have a letter and a basket. Would you be so kind as to take them to Hangzhou and send someone to deliver them to my family?” She handed him the letter. “Certainly. Where are the things?” “I have them,” the Seventh Lady answered for her. “When are you leaving, Mr Hu?” “The day after tomorrow.” “Then I shan't come to see you off.” “Please don't trouble yourself. What would you like me to bring back?” “Nothing comes to mind just now.” “Write to me if you think of anything. Or tell Seventh Sister.”

Once they had seen Luo into her carriage, the Seventh Lady hurried back inside and asked her husband, “What did she say in her letter?” “So Yingchun wielded the brush!” Hu said, a little surprised. “No wonder the handwriting looked familiar.” “I played the character-diviner for once. But I found it curious too. Why should she ask me to write such an entirely ordinary letter? What has become of whoever normally writes her letters home?” “There is certainly a reason. Tell me what was in it.” Gu could recite the whole letter from memory. When he had done so, he added, “One point is worth considering. She did not want to say explicitly that Little Uncle was bringing the letter and basket.” “Did she explain why she specifically wanted Mr Wu to write the reply?” “No.” Hu's question was different. “She has a daughter? She never told me.” “She has told you today, through Yingchun.” “Ah!” Gu understood. “So that is why she deliberately asked me to write it.”

“There are other reasons,” the Seventh Lady said. “First, she wants to see whether Little Uncle remembers old ties. You must have met her mother in the old days. If you remember them, you will go and see her.” “Of course. I had already decided to deliver the letter and things myself. With the festival coming, I must take a present too.” “That is the right thing to do. And she wants to test how you react when you see her daughter.” “Mm.” Hu nodded without committing himself. “Anything else?” Gu had used the phrase so often that day that it slipped out unconsciously. “She specified Mr Wu because she was afraid a character-diviner might not explain things clearly or write them properly, and might carelessly leave something out. Only Mr Wu can be relied upon.” Hu thought her reasoning entirely correct. After considering it for a while, he said with feeling, “Sister Luo's mind works very deeply.” “Deeply and quickly. I said that giving too little could cause offence; she said that giving too much could offend more than one person. Little Uncle, if you want this helper, whether the match succeeds will depend on the letter Mr Wu writes.” Hu understood. Back in Hangzhou, he first sent someone to attend to Luo's commission, adding a generous festival gift. Then, on a free day, he dressed simply, took few attendants and went in an easy manner to visit her mother. He addressed her by the old name, Auntie Luo, but she could scarcely recognize him. His unfamiliarity, added to her astonishment at the honour, made her extremely uneasy. Understanding her feelings, he began with news of her daughter, then gradually recalled old times. Only then did Auntie Luo relax. Once at ease, she naturally became both pleased and moved, repeatedly saying that she would never have dared imagine a man in his present position lowering himself to visit her.
